fields.title: Introducing aimbaza.org — the new MbazaNLP community hub
fields.excerpt: MbazaNLP has a new home. aimbaza.org brings together our models, datasets, events, and community resources in one place — built on Django and open-source from day one.
fields.body:
MbazaNLP has been building open-source NLP tools for Kinyarwanda and East African languages since its founding. Until now, our community presence has been spread across GitHub, HuggingFace, and a static website that was difficult to keep up to date.

Today we are launching aimbaza.org — a new community hub built on Django that brings everything together.

What's on the site

Projects & Models lists all 13 of our publicly available models across machine translation, speech recognition, text-to-speech, and conversational AI — all freely available on HuggingFace under open licences.

Opportunities surfaces grants, fellowships, and computing access (including DFKI HPC) relevant to African language NLP researchers.

Events will track past and upcoming workshops, sprints, and community calls.

The Gallery captures photos from our community events, starting with the Bakame Hackathon in April 2023.

Contribute explains how to get involved — whether through data, code, documentation, or community support.

Services & Offerings documents what MbazaNLP can offer to research partners and organisations looking to work with us.

Open infrastructure

The site is open-source and deployed from the MBAZA-NLP/aimbaza.org repository on GitHub. The CI/CD pipeline runs Black, Flake8, and automated tests on every pull request. We welcome contributions to the site itself — see the Contribute page for the pull request workflow.

What's next

In the coming weeks we will be adding a community blog with release notes for our models, technical posts from community members, and an events calendar. We are also building a Slack news bot that will post weekly digests of upcoming events and opportunities directly to our community workspace.

Join us on Slack at aimbaza.slack.com or browse the models at huggingface.co/mbazaNLP.

fields.title: Model documentation sprint: 13 HuggingFace improvements submitted
fields.excerpt: As part of the GIZ-funded community maintenance work, we submitted 13 pull requests across all MbazaNLP HuggingFace models and datasets, addressing every critical documentation gap found in the community audit.
fields.body:
As part of the GIZ-funded community maintenance contract, the first major work package was a systematic documentation audit and improvement sprint across all MbazaNLP models on HuggingFace.

The audit found that no model had a complete model card. Only 1 of 11 models had an Intended Use section. Several models had blank README files, and two had no card at all. We submitted 13 pull requests on 21 May 2026 covering every model and dataset in the mbazaNLP organisation.

What we fixed

Intended Use sections were added to all 10 models that were missing them. A clear statement of what a model is for — and what it should not be used for — is the most basic documentation requirement for responsible AI publishing.

Limitations and Bias & Fairness sections were added across all 13 models. Responsible disclosure of model limitations is a requirement under the HuggingFace Model Card specification.

BibTeX citation blocks were added to all 13 models. This makes it possible for researchers to cite MbazaNLP models in academic papers, which is important for the community's visibility and recognition in the research literature.

Code loading examples were added to three models that had none: bakame-chatbot-kinyarwanda, kinyarwanda-tts-model, and kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model. A model with no usage example is effectively inaccessible to practitioners who want to experiment with it.

Translation model code examples were updated for compatibility with Transformers v5. The previous examples used the v4 API, which fails for users installing the latest version of the library.

License conflicts were resolved in kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model, where the declared licence was inconsistent with the intended apache-2.0 release.

Numeric evaluation results were added to three quantized models that had no performance figures. A model card without metrics gives users no basis for comparing or selecting models.

Language tags were added to NLLB-Education, enabling the HuggingFace search system to surface the model to Kinyarwanda researchers.

Dataset improvements

PIQA-kin (a Kinyarwanda adaptation of the Physical Intuition Question Answering benchmark) received its first complete dataset card. The dataset had 100 downloads and 15 likes but no documentation. The new card describes the task, the data format, the collection process, and appropriate use cases.

NMT_Education_parallel_data_en_kin had a schema mismatch in its test split that was causing the HuggingFace dataset viewer to fail. The fix adds a configs/dataset_info YAML block with the correct column types, restoring the viewer for all users.

What's next

All 13 pull requests are open and awaiting merge by the respective model owners. If you own one of the mbazaNLP models, please review and merge your open PR — the links are in the community Slack #general channel.

In the next phase we will be publishing a standard model card template as a community resource on HuggingFace, so that all future MbazaNLP releases start from a complete, correctly formatted card rather than a blank README.

fields.title: Community update: aimbaza.org is live, engineering standards incoming, and a sprint in June
fields.excerpt: The new aimbaza.org site is now fully built and deployed to staging. Engineering standards are ready for publication. And we are running a community sprint on 14–15 June — open to all skill levels.
fields.body:
This is the second community release note from the GIZ-funded MbazaNLP maintenance work. It covers what has shipped since the model documentation sprint in May, what is coming next, and how to get involved.

aimbaza.org is feature-complete on staging

The replacement community website is now fully built and deployed to https://robo-advisor-4fl4.onrender.com. All nine planned pages are live:

Home and About carry over the community mission and partner acknowledgements. Projects & Models lists all 13 HuggingFace models and datasets with direct links. Community links out to Slack, GitHub, HuggingFace, and email. Events shows the community calendar plus a curated list of international AI and NLP events with sponsorship opportunities highlighted. Blog is where you are reading this. Opportunities lists computing access (Google TPU Research Cloud, AWS Research Credits), grants (Lacuna Fund, Mozilla Technology Fund, AI4D Africa, GIZ Digital Transformation), and fellowships (Masakhane, Google for Startups Africa). Contribute explains how to get involved with code, data, documentation, or community support. Services & Offerings describes what MbazaNLP can offer to research partners. Gallery shows photos from the Bakame Community Hackathon (April 2023).

The site is open-source at github.com/ronn13/aimbaza.org and will transfer to the MBAZA-NLP organisation once org admin access is confirmed. Production deployment to aimbaza.org is scheduled to follow immediately after that transfer.

Engineering standards

A Community Engineering Standards repository has been scaffolded covering Python style (Black, Flake8, PEP 8), git workflow (branch naming, commit conventions, PR process), model and dataset card requirements, repository naming conventions, and CI workflow templates. The repository is ready to publish to MBAZA-NLP/engineering-standards once the org admin creates the repo.

A model card template is also ready for publication to HuggingFace as mbazaNLP/model-card-template. This will ensure all future model releases start from a complete, correctly formatted card.

HuggingFace model card PRs — action still needed

The 13 pull requests submitted on 21 May are still open. If you are a model owner, your PR is waiting for your review. The list of open PRs and their URLs is in the first release note on this blog. Merging these PRs is the single highest-impact action any model owner can take right now — the documentation gaps are visible to every visitor who finds the models through HuggingFace search.

Join us: community sprint, 14–15 June 2026

We are running a two-day community sprint in Kigali on Saturday and Sunday, 14–15 June 2026. The sprint is open to all skill levels — NLP researchers, developers, translators, and anyone curious about Kinyarwanda language technology.

Planned activities include model evaluation sessions (testing the translation, ASR, and TTS models against real-world use cases), a data contribution track for adding parallel sentences to the NMT dataset, a documentation track for reviewing and improving model cards after the PRs merge, and an onboarding session for new contributors.

Details and sign-up will be posted in the #events channel on Slack. Join us at aimbaza.slack.com.

What's next

The remaining priorities for June are: production deployment of aimbaza.org once the repo transfer unblocks, publication of the engineering standards repository, the June sprint, and the final monthly progress report and handover documentation due 30 June 2026.

fields.title: What MbazaNLP has built: a guide to our open Kinyarwanda AI models
fields.excerpt: MbazaNLP has published 13 open-source AI models for Kinyarwanda and East African languages. This post maps the full landscape — what each model does, how to load it, and where it fits in an NLP pipeline.
fields.body:
MbazaNLP has been quietly building open-source AI infrastructure for Kinyarwanda and East African languages for several years. The result is 13 publicly available models on HuggingFace, spanning machine translation, speech recognition, text-to-speech, and conversational AI. This post provides a practical guide to what exists and how to use it.

All models are available at huggingface.co/mbazaNLP and are licensed under Apache 2.0 or compatible open licences unless stated otherwise.

Machine Translation

MbazaNLP has the largest set of open English-Kinyarwanda translation models of any public organisation. All are fine-tuned on Meta's NLLB-200 (No Language Left Behind) base model.

Nllb_finetuned_general_en_kin is the general-domain translation model, suitable for most use cases. Nllb_finetuned_education_en_kin and Nllb_finetuned_tourism_en_kin are domain-adapted versions that perform better on educational and tourism content respectively — a useful reminder that domain matters significantly for low-resource MT.

For deployment on constrained hardware, Quantized_Nllb_Finetuned_Edu_En_Kin_8bit and Quantized_Nllb_Finetuned_Tourism_En_Kin_8bit are 8-bit quantized versions of the education and tourism models, reducing memory requirements by roughly half with modest quality trade-offs.

NLLB-Education is a larger model providing higher-quality translation for the education domain, intended for production deployments where hardware is less constrained.

To load any translation model:

from transformers import pipeline
translator = pipeline('translation', model='mbazaNLP/Nllb_finetuned_general_en_kin')
result = translator('Hello, how are you?', src_lang='eng_Latn', tgt_lang='kin_Latn')
print(result[0]['translation_text'])

Speech Recognition (ASR)

Three ASR models cover Kinyarwanda with different architectures and trade-offs.

Whisper-Small-Kinyarwanda is a fine-tuned version of OpenAI's Whisper Small model. Note: the model was fine-tuned using language='sw' (Swahili) as the Whisper language tag — Kinyarwanda does not have its own tag in the base Whisper model. This is documented in the model card.

Kinyarwanda_nemo_stt_conformer_model uses NVIDIA's NeMo Conformer-CTC architecture, which tends to perform well on clean speech. stt_rw_sw_lg_conformer_ctc_large extends coverage to a multilingual model supporting Kinyarwanda, Swahili, and Luganda in a single checkpoint.

kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model uses Coqui STT (formerly Mozilla DeepSpeech). This was one of the earlier MbazaNLP models and demonstrates the community's work before the transition to Transformer-based architectures.

Text-to-Speech

kinyarwanda-tts-model provides Kinyarwanda speech synthesis. TTS for low-resource languages is significantly harder than ASR due to the need for high-quality single-speaker recordings, and this model represents a substantial data collection effort by the community.

Conversational AI

bakame-chatbot-kinyarwanda is the most-downloaded model in the MbazaNLP organisation. It powers the Bakame chatbot, a Kinyarwanda-language conversational AI that was the focus of the April 2023 Bakame Hackathon. The hackathon gathered community contributors to evaluate, extend, and improve the chatbot across a range of use cases.

Using the models

All models can be loaded with the HuggingFace Transformers library. The model cards on HuggingFace now include updated code examples following the recent documentation sprint. If you encounter any issues, open an issue on the relevant GitHub repository or post in the #models channel on our Slack workspace at aimbaza.slack.com.

Contributing

All models are open for improvement. If you have domain-specific data, evaluation benchmarks, or compute resources to contribute, we would like to hear from you. See the Contribute page on this site or reach out on Slack.

fields.title: Community update: eight weeks of infrastructure, a sprint, and what comes next
fields.excerpt: The GIZ-funded maintenance contract ends on 30 June. Here is what shipped across eight weeks — the new site, the Slack bot, the sprint, and what stays in place for the community to build on.
fields.body:
Eight weeks of infrastructure work closes on 30 June 2026. This post covers what was built, what the June sprint produced, and what is now in place for the community to sustain and grow independently.

aimbaza.org is live

The replacement community website is running in production at aimbaza.org. It was built from scratch on Django 4.2 and deployed on Render with a PostgreSQL database and a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline.

The site has thirteen pages: Home, Projects & Models, Events, Blog, Opportunities, Community, Partners, Gallery, Contribute, Services, and Demos. A few highlights:

  • Projects & Models catalogues all MbazaNLP models and datasets by task — machine translation, ASR, TTS, and chatbots — with direct links to HuggingFace.
  • Events shows a three-month community calendar plus a curated list of international AI and NLP events, updated weekly via a GitHub Actions workflow, with a filter for events that offer travel grants or sponsorship.
  • Opportunities lists computing access, grants, and fellowships relevant to African language NLP researchers, also updated automatically each week.
  • Partners now includes nine organisations: GIZ/FairForward, Digital Umuganda, University of Rwanda, CMU Africa, SheCanCode, kLab Rwanda, RISA, and Masakhane.

The site code is open-source. Contributions are welcome via the standard pull request workflow — see the Contribute page for setup instructions.

The June sprint

On 14 and 15 June 2026 we ran a two-day community sprint in Kigali across three contribution tracks.

Track A — Model evaluation tested the general, education, and tourism translation models and the Whisper-Small-Kinyarwanda ASR model against real-world inputs from participants. Participants rated each output on fluency, adequacy, and domain appropriateness. Results have been submitted as updated evaluation notes to the relevant model cards on HuggingFace.

Track B — Data contribution added new parallel sentence pairs to the NMT_Education_parallel_data_en_kin dataset. Contributions focused on the education domain and covered topics from primary school curricula. The batch pull request against the dataset has been submitted.

Track C — Documentation and onboarding reviewed the open model card pull requests submitted in May, walked first-time contributors through the GitHub and HuggingFace contribution workflow, and submitted fixes and improvements to the aimbaza.org site. Several participants made their first open-source contribution during the sprint.

Thank you to everyone who joined. The sprint technical brief — with full track descriptions and setup instructions — remains on the site for anyone who wants to run a similar session.

Model card PRs — all merged

All 13 model card pull requests submitted in May 2026 have now been merged by their respective model owners. Every MbazaNLP model on HuggingFace now has a complete card with Intended Use, Limitations, evaluation results, a working code example, and a BibTeX citation block. The checklist we published in Technical Post #3 — Writing better model cards for African NLP — is available for anyone publishing new models.

The Slack news bot

A GitHub Actions workflow posts a weekly digest to #general on the aimbaza Slack workspace every Monday. The digest covers upcoming events, new opportunities, and community announcements. It runs automatically and will continue after the contract ends — no manual work required to keep it going.

If you are not on Slack yet, join at the invite link.

Engineering standards — ready, pending publication

A Community Engineering Standards repository covering Python style, git workflow, model and dataset card standards, naming conventions, and CI workflow templates is fully written and ready to publish. Publication to MBAZA-NLP/engineering-standards is pending the creation of the repository by the organisation admin. This will be completed as soon as that access is confirmed.

What stays in place

The following infrastructure is running autonomously and will continue after the contract closes:

  • aimbaza.org — production site on Render, auto-deploys from the main branch on GitHub
  • Slack news bot — weekly digest every Monday, fortnightly community digest every other Monday
  • Opportunities auto-refresh — GitHub Actions updates the opportunities list every Monday morning
  • Events auto-refresh — GitHub Actions updates the international events list every Monday morning
  • CI/CD pipeline — lint, tests, and coverage check run on every pull request to the site repository

Ownership of the Render hosting, Namecheap domain, Slack workspace, and GitHub repository will be transferred to the incoming community maintainer(s) before 30 June 2026.

How to stay involved

  • Join Slack at aimbaza.slack.com for weekly updates and community discussion
  • Contribute to the site — open an issue or submit a pull request at the aimbaza.org repository
  • Contribute data — the NMT education dataset welcomes new parallel sentence pairs via pull request
  • Use the models — all MbazaNLP models are open and available at huggingface.co/mbazaNLP
  • Reach out — for partnerships or collaboration, email mbazanlp.community@gmail.com

fields.title: Writing better model cards for African NLP: lessons from 13 pull requests
fields.excerpt: Before May 2026, not one of MbazaNLP’s 13 publicly available models had a complete HuggingFace model card. Here is what we fixed across 13 pull requests, and a checklist so your next model release starts from a better baseline.
fields.body:
Before May 2026, not one of MbazaNLP’s 13 publicly available models had a complete HuggingFace model card. Here is what we fixed across 13 pull requests, and a checklist so your next model release starts from a better baseline.

The cost of a blank model card

If you have published a model on HuggingFace and left the README blank, you are not alone. Across the 13 publicly available models in the MbazaNLP organisation none had a complete model card before May 2026, seven had no Intended Use section, two had entirely blank README files. And one model had accumulated 15,000 downloads with no documentation at all.

Responsible AI publishing requires disclosing what a model is for, what it should not be used for, and what its limitations are. Without that information, users cannot assess fit-for-purpose, harmful misuse goes undisclosed, and researchers cannot cite the work in academic papers. For communities building language technology for underrepresented languages, every undiscoverable or uncitable model makes it harder to attract collaborators, funding, and downstream use.

Between 21 and 27 May 2026, we submitted 13 pull requests across all MbazaNLP models and datasets. This post covers the five most common gaps we found, how we fixed them, and a minimal-but-complete model card template you can use for your next release.

What a complete HuggingFace model card actually requires

The HuggingFace Model Card specification has two layers: the machine-readable YAML frontmatter and human-readable prose sections. Most practitioners fill in some prose and miss the YAML — which is exactly what HuggingFace uses to surface models in search and filter results.

The YAML frontmatter should include:

  • Language — a BCP-47 language code (e.g. rw for Kinyarwanda, sw for Swahili)
  • License — the SPDX identifier (e.g. apache-2.0, mit)
  • Tags — task categories (e.g. translation, automatic-speech-recognition, text-to-speech)

The prose sections should cover:

  • Model description — what it is, architecture, and base model
  • Intended Use — primary use cases and out-of-scope uses
  • Limitations and Bias — known failure modes and fairness considerations
  • Training data — dataset name, size, and source
  • Evaluation results — at least one metric on a named test set
  • How to use — a working code example
  • Citation — a BibTeX entry

A model without language tags is invisible to the HuggingFace search system, and a model without a citation block cannot be credited in academic work.

The five most common gaps in the community

Missing Intended Use. The most frequent gap across all 13 models — seven of eleven had no Intended Use section at all. This section is two short paragraphs: what the model is designed for, and what it should not be used for. A general-domain translation model is not appropriate for medical or legal translation, and that needs to be stated explicitly.

No evaluation metrics. Three of our quantized translation models had no performance figures of any kind, giving users no basis for comparison or selection. A single BLEU score on a named test set is more informative than nothing.

Missing or wrong language tags in YAML frontmatter. NLLB-Education, a Kinyarwanda translation model with significant community uptake, had no language tags in its YAML frontmatter. HuggingFace uses these tags to populate the “Models for Kinyarwanda” search results. Without them, the model is effectively invisible to any researcher who searches by language rather than by name. The fix is one line of YAML: language: [rw, en].

Outdated code examples. Two translation models had code examples written for the Transformers v4 API. These examples fail silently on v5, which is what most users will have installed today. Always test the code example in your card against the current library version before publishing.

No citation block. None of the 13 models had a BibTeX entry, making it difficult for models to be cited or credited in academic work — an issue low-resource language communities need to stay on top of, since research output and funding often depend on citation counts.

What a minimal complete card looks like

Below is a stripped-down but complete model card for a fictional MbazaNLP-style translation model. Every required section is present; none is padded.

---
language:
  - rw
  - en
license: apache-2.0
tags:
  - translation
  - kinyarwanda
metrics:
  - bleu
---

# MbazaNLP Example Translation Model

## Model description
Fine-tuned on Meta NLLB-200 for English-Kinyarwanda translation in the general domain.

## Intended use
Primary use: English-to-Kinyarwanda translation of general-domain text.
Out-of-scope: Medical, legal, or safety-critical translation without human review.

## Limitations and bias
Performance degrades on technical or domain-specific vocabulary not present in training data.
The model inherits biases present in the NLLB-200 base model.

## Training data
Fine-tuned on the MbazaNLP parallel corpus (en-rw), 120,000 sentence pairs.

## Evaluation results
| Test set          | BLEU |
|-------------------|------|
| flores200-rw-dev  | 28.4 |

## How to use
from transformers import pipeline
translator = pipeline('translation', model='mbazaNLP/example-model')
result = translator('Hello.', src_lang='eng_Latn', tgt_lang='kin_Latn')
print(result[0]['translation_text'])

## Citation
@misc{mbazanlp2026example,
  author = {MbazaNLP Community},
  title  = {Example Translation Model},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://huggingface.co/mbazaNLP/example-model}
}

The MbazaNLP model card template

To make it easier for future MbazaNLP releases to start from a complete card, we have prepared a community model card template available in the mbazaNLP organisation on HuggingFace. It includes pre-filled YAML frontmatter with all required fields, placeholder text for each prose section, an annotated code example block, an evaluation results table, and a BibTeX stub.

Fork the template when starting a new model release, fill in the sections, and submit a pull request to your model repository. The template is licensed CC-BY, so it can be adapted for other communities and language families.

Checklist

Copy this into your next model card PR description and work through it before opening the pull request:

  • YAML frontmatter: language (BCP-47 codes), license (SPDX), task tags
  • Model description: architecture, base model, what it does
  • Intended Use: primary use (1 paragraph) + out-of-scope uses (1 paragraph)
  • Limitations and Bias: at least one paragraph on known failure modes
  • Training data: dataset name, size, and source
  • Evaluation results: at least one metric on a named test set in a table
  • How to use: working code example tested against the current library version
  • Citation: BibTeX entry with author, title, year, and URL

Why this matters for African NLP

Low-resource languages are underrepresented in NLP research partly because the tooling is hard to find and hard to trust. A well-documented model is more likely to be downloaded, cited, built upon, and improved. It is also more likely to attract the attention of funders, collaborators, and researchers who are looking for a foundation to build on.

The 13 pull requests submitted in May 2026 are one community’s attempt to close a documentation gap that had been accumulating for years. The model card template and this checklist are how other communities can avoid starting from the same baseline. If you maintain a model for Kinyarwanda, Swahili, Luganda, or any other African language, the checklist above takes less than an hour to work through — and that hour is the difference between a model researchers can discover, evaluate, and cite, and one that sits invisible in a repository.
